top_stories.headline: Hollywood's Golden Age Loses One of Its Last Stars: Eva Marie Saint Dies at 102
top_stories.deck: The Oscar-winning actress of 'On the Waterfront' and 'North by Northwest' died of natural causes at her Los Angeles home.
top_stories.body:
Eva Marie Saint, the luminous actress who won an Academy Award in her very first film and went on to become one of Hollywood's most enduring stars, died Tuesday at her home in Los Angeles. She was 102. Her publicist said she died of natural causes, surrounded by family.

Born on the Fourth of July, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, Saint built her career in live television and on Broadway before director Elia Kazan cast her opposite Marlon Brando in 1954's 'On the Waterfront.' Playing Edie Doyle, the strong-willed Catholic schoolgirl seeking justice for her murdered brother, Saint won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in 1955 — accepting the award just days before giving birth to her first child.

Five years later she transformed into the cool double agent Eve Kendall opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock's 'North by Northwest,' cementing her place among the great screen performers of the 1950s. She worked with a procession of legendary directors after that, from Otto Preminger on 'Exodus' to Norman Jewison on 'The Russians Are Coming.'

After marrying director Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, Saint deliberately stepped back from film to raise her children, returning to television in the 1970s and winning an Emmy in 1990 for the miniseries 'People Like Us.' Her seven-decade career spanned more than 160 productions, and she was among the last surviving stars of Hollywood's Golden Age.

top_stories.headline: Trump Approves Firing Squad Execution for Fort Hood Shooter Nidal Hasan
top_stories.deck: If carried out, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 — but the Army has yet to announce a date.
top_stories.body:
President Donald Trump has approved execution by firing squad for Nidal Hasan, the former Army major convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13 people and wounded 32. The approval, made on the recommendation of the defense secretary, moves one of the military's longest-running death penalty cases toward its final chapter.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Texas base on November 5, 2009, and was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013. His appeals stretched more than a decade until the Supreme Court declined to hear his petition in March 2025, leaving the sentence intact.

If the execution goes ahead, it would be the first carried out by the U.S. military since 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth — and the military's first firing-squad execution since World War II. CBS News reported an internal email pointed to December 3, though the Army has not publicly confirmed any date; the Secretary of the Army must still set the time and place.

The case has long been tangled in the debate over how the government labels jihadist attacks on American soil. The Obama administration initially described the shooting as workplace violence, while Hasan himself described it as retaliation for U.S. wars in the Muslim world.

top_stories.headline: Eagles Great Lane Johnson Walks Away at 36 to Focus on Mental Health
top_stories.deck: The six-time Pro Bowler and two-time Super Bowl champion retires after 14 seasons, all of them in Philadelphia.
top_stories.body:
Philadelphia Eagles right tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement Tuesday, ending a 14-year career spent entirely in Philadelphia. The 36-year-old said he wants to focus on his mental health and his family.

“I deeply wanted to gut it out for one more year, to take the field with my brothers for one last season,” Johnson wrote in a statement. “But after a lot of reflection, I've realized that my personal and family priorities in my life have changed. Right now, it is critical that I focus on my mental health.”

Johnson, the fourth overall pick in the 2013 draft, started 171 regular-season games and 15 more in the playoffs, earning six Pro Bowl selections and first-team All-Pro honors in 2017 and 2022. He won two Super Bowl rings with the Eagles and was unexpectedly scratched from Sunday's loss to the Rams for personal reasons.

Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie called him “an all-time Eagle and one of the best players ever to play his position in NFL history,” adding there is no doubt Johnson will one day reach the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Johnson took a leave of absence during the 2021 season while battling anxiety and depression, and has since become one of the league's most prominent advocates for mental health awareness.

top_stories.headline: Separatists Return to Power in Quebec — But Fall Short of a Majority
top_stories.deck: The Parti Québécois won Monday's provincial election and promises another independence referendum, though only about 30% of Quebecers back leaving Canada.
top_stories.body:
The separatist Parti Québécois won Quebec's provincial election Monday, returning to power for the first time in more than a decade with a promise to hold another referendum on independence from Canada. But the party fell five seats short of a majority, winning 59 of the 127 seats in the National Assembly.

Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged voters had denied him a majority: “Quebecers elected the Parti Québécois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message.” The outgoing governing party, the Coalition Avenir Québec, lost every seat it held — all 79 of them.

St-Pierre Plamondon has pledged an independence referendum but says he would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. Still, a McGill political scientist notes the win reflects Quebec's fractured multiparty system more than a separatist surge: support for independence sits near 30%, low by historical standards.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who remains popular in Quebec, congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and signaled Ottawa would work with the incoming government. The result lands two weeks before Albertans vote October 19 on whether to hold their own separation referendum.

top_stories.headline: ABC Asks Federal Judge to Block Trump's FCC From Early License Review
top_stories.deck: The network calls the accelerated review of eight station licenses retaliation for coverage the president dislikes; a ruling isn't expected before mid-October.
top_stories.body:
A lawyer for ABC asked a federal judge Tuesday to block the Trump administration from conducting an unusual early review of the network's broadcast licenses — likening it to a looming execution by guillotine that is already chilling ABC's editorial decisions just weeks before the U.S. midterm elections.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan did not immediately rule on ABC's request for a preliminary injunction. The network argues the review is unconstitutional, a violation of free speech, and retaliation for content President Donald Trump dislikes. A government attorney countered that the court lacks jurisdiction because the case belongs in a different venue, and said ABC failed to show irreparable harm.

ABC and its parent company Disney sued the FCC and Commissioner Brendan Carr in August, months after the commission ordered eight ABC-owned stations to submit license renewal applications years ahead of schedule — renewals not otherwise due until October 2028. The judge asked both sides to file additional arguments by October 9 and October 14, with no ruling expected before mid-October.

The case is one of several ongoing legal battles between the administration and news outlets, including the Associated Press, over coverage of and access to the executive branch.
